title: Help map the cameras
description: How to contribute careful camera observations to the community map.
body_md:
## Recognize a possible plate reader

[EDIT ME: verify for this campaign] An ALPR, or automated license plate reader, is a camera system that reads vehicle license plates. Its shape, a roadside placement or a solar panel alone does not show that a camera is an ALPR. Compare what you see with the known ALPR and non-ALPR examples on the [OpenStreetMap wiki](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:surveillance:type=ALPR), and leave an uncertain camera for a knowledgeable mapper.

## Stay safe and protect privacy

[EDIT ME: verify for this campaign] Stay on public property, do not touch equipment, and never photograph people or license plates. Note only where a camera is and what is plainly visible from where you stand. Do not share anything that identifies a person.

## Add a missing camera

[EDIT ME: verify for this campaign] You can add a point with an OpenStreetMap account and an editor, or through the DeFlock reporting page at https://deflock.me/report, which uses OpenStreetMap data and asks for an OpenStreetMap account. Look at the existing points first, then add one node at the camera you observed, tagged `man_made=surveillance` and `surveillance:type=ALPR` (capital letters matter), as the [surveillance wiki page](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:man_made=surveillance) describes. Add the manufacturer and the operator only if you know them: the operator is the organization that runs the camera, not the company that made it, and it should never be guessed from a city boundary or a brand. This tool never edits OpenStreetMap, uploads a report or fetches during a build, so a new point shows on this site only after an organizer refreshes the map data and builds.

## Correct an existing point

[EDIT ME: verify for this campaign] If a point is in the wrong place or has a wrong tag, correct that existing node instead of adding a duplicate. The OpenStreetMap wiki also describes tags such as the public or outdoor setting and the surveillance zone, which are wiki guidance. This campaign's map reads only the two tags named above, plus the manufacturer and operator when present.

## Understand ownership unconfirmed

[EDIT ME: verify for this campaign] Community-mapped points; ownership unconfirmed. A point or a count is a volunteer's observation, not proof of which agency owns or runs a camera, what it captures, whether it is legal or that any rule was broken. An operator tag is a mapper's entry, not independent verification.

## Understand campaign point checks

[EDIT ME: verify for this campaign] A point check is a dated, sourced note by an organizer about one mapped point. It is not a reviewed finding and has not been through the review described on the How to read our findings page (methods.html). The check `seen_in_person` means an organizer saw a camera there, and `in_agency_record` means an agency record lists the point, which does not establish who owns it. The checks `not_found_on_site` and `duplicate` keep the point on the map and in every count.
